results.topic: How a vaccine trains the immune system

deck.title: How a vaccine trains the immune system
deck.subtitle: 5 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: A tiny, harmless piece of a virus is injected into the body.
items.why: This acts as a preview, letting the defense network study the threat without facing an actual infection.
items.scene: A tiny, harmless toy robot shaped like a virus sits politely on a velvet cushion.

check.wrong: The injection contains a weakened live virus that always causes a mild version of the disease.
check.right: The injection only contains a harmless fragment or blueprint, never the whole live virus.

items.link: Triggers the guard cells

items.answer: Specialized guard cells spot the foreign piece and raise the alarm.
items.why: The immune system constantly patrols for strangers, and any unrecognized shape instantly commands attention.
items.scene: A wide-eyed guard owl blows a giant brass trumpet upon seeing the toy robot.
items.link: Recruits the master molders

items.answer: Special cells called lymphocytes design custom proteins called antibodies to fit the intruder.
items.why: Every invader requires a bespoke molecular handcuffs shape to neutralize it effectively.
items.scene: Busy dwarf blacksmiths hammer glowing metal keys specifically shaped to lock the toy robot.

check.wrong: The body uses leftover generic antibodies from previous colds to fight the new vaccine.
check.right: The immune system manufactures brand-new, customized antibodies exclusively shaped for this specific threat.

items.link: Stores the memory blueprints

items.answer: Long-lasting memory cells retain the exact blueprint of the intruder's shape for decades.
items.why: Without these archives, the body would forget the lesson and have to start from scratch next time.
items.scene: An old librarian carefully slides a glowing blueprint scroll into a vault marked with a shield.

check.wrong: Antibodies float freely in the bloodstream forever, constantly searching for invaders.
check.right: Antibodies fade away over time, but memory cells remain ready to quickly produce more when needed.

items.link: Defeats real invaders instantly

items.answer: If the real virus ever attacks, memory cells recognize it and destroy it before illness starts.
items.why: Previous training allows a lightning-fast response that stops the pathogen from multiplying.
items.scene: A lightning bolt instantly zaps a real green monster before it can take a single step.

check.wrong: Vaccines create an impenetrable physical shield that prevents viruses from ever entering the body.
check.right: Vaccines let viruses enter, but destroy them so rapidly that you never experience symptoms.

check.right: Plants build every single molecule of sugar themselves from thin air and water.

results.topic: What caused the 1929 stock market crash

deck.title: Causes of the 1929 Stock Market Crash
deck.subtitle: 5 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Easy credit allowed ordinary people to buy stocks with borrowed money, driving prices far above actual value.
items.why: Investors relied on continuous price increases to pay back loans, creating an extremely fragile financial house of cards.
items.scene: A towering castle built entirely of stacked playing cards wobbles violently as a golden hand places one more card on top.

check.wrong: The crash happened because the government suddenly outlawed all stock trading overnight.
check.right: The crash happened because asset prices detached from reality and panic selling suddenly overwhelmed the market.

items.link: Leads to widespread overleveraging across the entire economy

items.answer: Investors bought stocks using as little as ten percent cash down, borrowing the remaining ninety percent from brokers.
items.why: This extreme leverage magnified potential profits, but it also meant a tiny price drop would wipe out the investor entirely.
items.scene: A tightrope walker holds a tiny paper umbrella while balancing on a single thread suspended over a roaring canyon.

check.wrong: Buying on margin meant people were purchasing groceries on credit rather than actual investments.
check.right: Buying on margin meant purchasing stocks with borrowed money using the purchased shares as collateral.

items.link: Triggers sudden margin calls when stock prices dip

items.answer: As stock prices slipped slightly, lenders demanded immediate loan repayments, forcing investors to dump shares frantically.
items.why: Panic feeds on itself in financial markets, turning a routine market correction into a self-reinforcing downward spiral.
items.scene: Thousands of identical penguins panic on an ice floe, all diving off the edge into the dark water at the exact same moment.

check.wrong: Brokers bought up all the remaining shares to protect their clients from losing any money.
check.right: Brokers demanded immediate cash repayment of loans, forcing panic selling to cover debts.

items.link: Causes widespread bank failures due to unpaid loans

items.answer: Unpaid loans crushed banks that had lent money to speculators, causing frightened depositors to withdraw all their cash.
items.why: Banks keep only a fraction of deposits on hand, so a sudden rush of withdrawals rapidly exhausts their liquid reserves.
items.scene: A massive honey jar cracks down the middle, and golden honey streams out onto the floor while panicked bees swarm around it.

check.wrong: Banks simply closed their doors voluntarily because the bankers wanted to take a long vacation.
check.right: Banks failed because borrowers defaulted on loans and panicked depositors rushed to withdraw their funds simultaneously.

items.link: Results in a severe contraction of the money supply

items.answer: The collapse of the banking system froze credit, plunging businesses into bankruptcy and starting the Great Depression.
items.why: Without functioning credit and circulating money, commerce grinds to a halt, destroying jobs and consumer spending power.
items.scene: A giant grandfather clock freezes mid-tick, its heavy golden pendulum locking completely in place as dust settles over the gears.

check.wrong: The economy recovered within a single weekend as international trade immediately doubled.
check.right: The economy contracted severely, leading to a decade of high unemployment and stagnant business activity.

results.topic: How compound interest grows savings over time

deck.title: How compound interest grows savings
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Your deposited money earns a percentage based on the starting balance over a set time period.
items.why: Banks pay you to use your money, providing a baseline return that fuels future growth.
items.scene: A shiny gold coin sits on a table, slowly sweating a smaller silver coin next to itself.

check.wrong: Interest is calculated using the total amount currently in the account including previous earnings.
check.right: Initial interest is calculated only on the original deposit amount during the first cycle.

items.link: adds earnings back into the balance

items.answer: The interest earned in the first period is added directly to your original starting balance.
items.why: Merging earnings with the base amount increases the total size of the pot for the next calculation.
items.scene: A tiny silver coin melts into the gold coin, visibly swelling the original coin to a larger size.

check.wrong: The interest earned is automatically sent to a separate account so the main balance never changes.
check.right: The interest earned is merged directly into the main balance to increase the total amount.

items.link: enables earning interest on interest

items.answer: The next interest payment is calculated using the new, larger total including past earnings.
items.why: A larger base number naturally produces a bigger payout when multiplied by the exact same percentage rate.
items.scene: The swollen gold coin drops bigger rain droplets of silver onto the table below.

check.wrong: Interest payments stay the exact same size every single period because the percentage rate increases.
check.right: Interest payments grow larger each period because the base amount being multiplied keeps increasing.

items.link: accelerates the overall growth rate

items.answer: The speed of wealth accumulation accelerates rapidly over time as earnings continuously compound upon themselves.
items.why: Cumulative layering creates a curve that shoots upward steeply rather than growing in a straight, predictable line.
items.scene: A tiny snowball rolls down a short hill, instantly transforming into a massive boulder crushing a fence.

check.wrong: Savings grow in a straight, steady diagonal line where the exact same amount is added every year.
check.right: Savings grow in an accelerating curve where the amount added gets bigger every single year.

check.right: Spreading money reduces specific company risk, but overall market drops can still affect value.

items.answer: As the overall economy grows and companies make profits, the total value of your fund steadily rises.

check.right: Index fund returns fluctuate daily based on the actual performance of the underlying companies.

results.topic: How a UPI payment moves money between two bank accounts

deck.title: How a UPI payment moves money
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: The payer scans a QR code using a mobile app to capture the receiver's virtual payment address.
items.why: This address acts as a secure alias protecting the actual bank account numbers from exposure during transactions.

check.wrong: Entering your PIN tells the merchant your actual bank password so they can withdraw the money.
check.right: Entering your PIN authorizes your own bank to securely release the funds for this single transaction.

items.link: Triggers communication between both banks.

items.answer: A central payment switch receives the encrypted message and routes the debit and credit instructions.

check.wrong: The central switch holds all your money in a giant digital wallet before sending it onward.
check.right: The central switch only passes messages between banks; it never actually holds your money.

items.scene: Two giant mechanical scales balance out instantly as gold coins magically vanish from one side and appear on the other.

results.topic: How a contract is formed: offer, acceptance and consideration

deck.title: How a contract is formed
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: One party proposes a clear promise to do or provide something specific to another party.
items.why: Clear terms are essential because both people must know exactly what they are agreeing to trade.
items.scene: A giant glowing neon sign hovers in the air, spelling out an offer to sell a bicycle for fifty dollars.

check.wrong: Any casual mention of selling an item in a conversation legally counts as a binding offer.
check.right: Only a specific, serious proposal intended to create legal obligations counts as a valid offer.

items.link: The offer travels across the room to the second person.

items.answer: The second party agrees completely to the exact terms of the proposal without changing them.
items.why: Mirroring the exact terms ensures both minds meet on the exact same agreement.
items.scene: A massive heavy stamp slams down on a floating paper, stamping the word accepted in bright green ink.

check.wrong: Accepting an offer while changing some of the conditions still creates a valid legal agreement.

items.link: Acceptance triggers the exchange of value.

items.scene: Two robotic hands swap a shiny gold coin for a heavy iron key in midair.

check.wrong: Giving a simple free promise without expecting anything in return creates a legally binding contract.
check.right: A promise to make a gift without any return value is not enforceable as a contract.

items.link: The completed exchange locks the agreement into place.

items.answer: Both parties intend for their agreed exchange to carry serious legal consequences if broken.
items.why: This mutual understanding transforms a simple social promise into a legally protected agreement.
items.scene: A glowing glass shield snaps shut around the participants, sealing their agreement into solid law.

check.wrong: Friends making a casual weekend dinner promise automatically form a legally binding contract.
check.right: Social and domestic promises lack the intent to create legal relations, so they are not contracts.

results.topic: How HTTPS keeps a connection private

deck.title: How HTTPS keeps a connection private
deck.subtitle: 5 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Your browser starts the secure connection by saying hello and sharing supported security codes.
items.why: This handshake begins the process of establishing trust and encryption parameters before any data moves.
items.scene: A tiny knight knocks on a giant glowing castle door, holding up a list of secret handshakes.

check.wrong: Your browser sends your actual password during this first greeting to prove who you are.
check.right: Your browser only sends a random number and supported security codes, never your password.

items.link: Server replies with its digital certificate

items.answer: The website replies with its digital certificate to prove its true identity.
items.why: Websites must prove they are who they claim to be so you do not accidentally send data to an impostor.
items.scene: The castle guard holds up an official royal passport stamped by a trusted kingdom authority.

check.wrong: The website certificate is just a simple password created by the website owner yesterday.
check.right: The certificate is a cryptographic document verified by a trusted third-party organization.

items.link: Browser verifies the certificate

items.answer: Your browser checks if a trusted authority vouches for the website certificate.
items.why: If the validator is unknown, your browser warns you that the connection might be unsafe.
items.scene: A wise owl inspects the royal passport with a magnifying glass, checking the official wax seal.

check.wrong: Your browser calls the website owner directly on the phone to confirm their identity.
check.right: Your browser mathematically verifies pre-installed digital signatures from trusted security companies.

items.link: Both create a secret key

items.answer: Both sides use a secure math trick to create a shared secret key.
items.why: This temporary key is known only to your device and the server, keeping hackers completely blind.

results.topic: How a large language model predicts the next word

deck.title: How a language model predicts words
deck.subtitle: 5 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: The model splits incoming text into smaller chunks called tokens, which can be words or parts of words.
items.why: Computers cannot process raw human letters directly, so converting text into numerical tokens is the necessary first step.
items.scene: A giant paper shredder chops sentences into colorful numbered puzzle pieces floating in the air.

check.wrong: Large language models read human sentences just like people do, word by word.
check.right: Models actually read text as numerical codes representing fragments of words called tokens.

items.link: Converts tokens into dense numerical coordinates

items.answer: Each token is converted into a vector, which is a long list of numbers representing its meaning.
items.why: Numbers allow the computer to calculate relationships, placing words with similar meanings close together in a geometric space.
items.scene: Thousands of glowing glowing coordinates shifting like stars inside a giant 3D transparent globe.

check.wrong: Words are stored inside the computer as exact dictionary definitions and rigid rulebooks.
check.right: Words are translated into floating numerical coordinates that represent their contextual meanings.

items.link: Passes vectors through attention layers

items.answer: Attention mechanisms calculate how strongly every token relates to all other tokens in the prompt.
items.why: This allows the model to understand ambiguous words by looking at surrounding clues, like knowing a bank refers to a river.
items.scene: A bustling switchboard operator with a thousand glowing telephone wires connecting words across the room.

check.wrong: Every word in a sentence has an isolated meaning regardless of the surrounding text.
check.right: The meaning of each token shifts dynamically based on surrounding context and relationships.

items.link: Calculates probabilities for candidate tokens

items.answer: The model scores every possible vocabulary token to determine how likely it is to appear next.
items.why: These raw scores, called logits, reflect patterns learned from reading billions of pages of human writing.
items.scene: A massive horse race starting gate where thousands of numbered horses strain forward in neon lights.

check.wrong: The computer invents completely original thoughts from scratch without relying on past statistics.
check.right: The model calculates statistical probabilities of the next token based on learned writing patterns.

items.link: Selects the final output token

items.answer: The model picks one token from the probability distribution and adds it to the output text.
items.why: Repeating this single step one word at a time allows the system to generate coherent paragraphs.
items.scene: A mechanical stamping press slamming down to print a single glowing word onto an endless scroll.

check.wrong: The model writes an entire paragraph all at once in a single creative flash.
check.right: The model generates text strictly one token at a time in a continuous loop.

results.topic: How Git records and merges changes

deck.title: How Git records and merges changes
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Git saves a snapshot of your project files as a commit object when you explicitly record changes.
items.why: Snapshots let you travel back in time to any previous state without storing duplicate files.
items.scene: A glowing camera takes a 3D hologram of a desk covered in papers.

check.wrong: Git records every single keystroke you make as you type your code.
check.right: Git only records snapshots when you explicitly choose to save a commit.

items.link: pushes the snapshot onto a timeline branch

items.answer: A branch points to a specific commit, creating an independent line of development.
items.why: Branches allow you to build new features safely without breaking the main working code.
items.scene: A glowing tree branch splits into two separate glowing paths in mid-air.

check.wrong: Branches create entirely separate physical copies of your project folder on your computer.
check.right: Branches are just lightweight movable pointers pointing to specific commits.

items.link: leads to making changes on the new branch

items.answer: Git combines the history of two different branches when you ask to bring changes together.
items.why: Merging unites separate efforts into a single unified version of the project.
items.scene: Two separate glowing rivers flow together into one wide, bright stream.

check.wrong: Merging automatically rewrites all older history to match the newest branch.
check.right: Merging creates a new commit that combines the histories of both branches.

items.link: triggers an automatic comparison of the files

items.answer: Git pauses and asks you to manually choose which changes to keep when edits overlap.
items.why: Computers cannot safely guess your design intent when two people edit the exact same line.
items.scene: A giant glowing traffic cop stops two trains heading toward the same track.

check.wrong: Git randomly deletes one of the conflicting edits to finish the merge automatically.
check.right: Git pauses the merge and makes you manually choose which version to keep.

results.topic: How a refrigerator keeps food cold

deck.title: How a refrigerator keeps food cold
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: An electric compressor squeezes the refrigerant gas, raising its temperature and pressure.
items.why: Compressing a gas forces its molecules closer together, which rapidly generates heat energy.
items.scene: A giant silver fist inside the fridge wall crushes a cloud of glowing blue gas into a tiny, hot glowing ball.

check.wrong: The compressor creates cold air directly and blows it into the food compartments.
check.right: The compressor only pressurizes gas to change its temperature and drive the cooling cycle.

items.link: pushes the hot gas into the condenser coils

items.answer: The hot gas flows through coils outside the back, releasing its heat into the room.
items.why: Heat naturally moves from a warmer area to a cooler room, turning the gas into a liquid.
items.scene: A copper snake on the back of the fridge sweats glowing red droplets of pure heat onto the kitchen floor.

check.wrong: The coils absorb heat from the kitchen to keep the outside walls warm.
check.right: The coils expel heat from inside the fridge out into the surrounding room.

items.link: flows liquid refrigerant to the expansion valve

items.answer: The liquid passes through a tiny valve, causing its pressure and temperature to drop sharply.
items.why: Rapid expansion forces the liquid to instantly cool down well below freezing point.
items.scene: A microscopic bouncer guards a narrow doorway, spraying a freezing cold mist of sparkling diamond dust.

check.wrong: The valve adds cold chemicals to the liquid to make it lose its heat.
check.right: The sudden drop in pressure alone causes the liquid to become extremely cold.

items.link: feeds the freezing liquid into evaporator coils

items.answer: The freezing liquid flows through coils inside the fridge, absorbing heat from your food.
items.why: Heat from inside the fridge transfers into the cold liquid, boiling it back into a gas.
items.scene: An iceberg shaped like a sponge inside the walls eagerly drinks up red waves of heat radiating from milk cartons.

check.wrong: The fridge creates coldness by pumping ice-cold air from a hidden freezer block.
check.right: The fridge removes heat by letting evaporating liquid absorb warmth from the interior.

deck.title: How a flush toilet works

items.answer: Pushing the handle rotates a metal arm inside the tank.
items.why: This mechanical rotation lifts the connected chain, which pulls the flapper plug open.
items.scene: A tiny crane operator inside the ceramic tank pulls a heavy steel lever to lift a rubber seal.

check.wrong: The handle directly pushes water down the drain using air pressure.
check.right: The handle only lifts a plug to release water stored in the tank.

items.why: Rapid volume overwhelms the trapway, creating a sudden surge that initiates the siphon effect.
items.scene: A waterfall of crystal clear water plunges from a high cliff into a porcelain canyon.

check.wrong: The water is pumped into the bowl under high pressure from the city mains.
check.right: The water falls entirely by gravity from the tank above.

items.why: This suction pulls bowl contents downward and over the bend faster than normal gravity flow.
items.scene: A giant invisible vacuum cleaner sucks everything out of the bowl through a curved glass tube.

check.wrong: Waste is pushed down the drain purely by the physical force of the falling water.
check.right: Waste is pulled down by a vacuum suction created in the curved pipe.

items.link: empties the bowl

items.answer: As water level drops, a hollow plastic float falls and opens the fill valve.
items.why: Fresh water rushes in to refill both the tank and the bowl for the next flush.

check.wrong: The toilet refills itself automatically using moisture pulled from the bathroom air.
check.right: The toilet refills using fresh water from the building supply pipe.

results.topic: How noise-cancelling headphones work

deck.title: How noise-cancelling headphones work
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: A tiny microphone on the outside of the ear cup listens to ambient noise in the room.
items.why: The system must intercept sound waves before they reach your eardrum to neutralize them in time.
items.scene: A tiny metal ear with a giant golden hearing horn strapped to the outside, greedily swallowing room sounds.

check.wrong: The microphone blocks sound physically by acting like a tiny soundproof wall.
check.right: The microphone only records the sound waves to send them into a tiny computer chip.

items.link: Sends the audio wave to the internal microchip.

items.answer: A digital processor flips the recorded sound wave upside down to create an exact opposite wave.
items.why: An inverted wave mirrors the original, matching every peak with a valley and every valley with a peak.
items.scene: An acrobat standing on the ceiling inside the headphone cup, perfectly mirroring every move of a dancer below.

check.wrong: The chip deletes the sound wave by multiplying its volume by zero instantly.
check.right: The chip creates a mathematical mirror image of the sound wave without erasing anything yet.

items.link: Pumps the inverted wave into the speaker driver.

items.answer: The headphone speaker plays this flipped wave, known as anti-noise, directly into your ear canal.
items.why: Sound waves can overlap and combine, a physical property known as superposition that alters total volume.
items.scene: A cheerful ghost blowing soap bubbles that pop and swallow incoming room noise like tiny vacuum cleaners.

check.wrong: The speaker blasts loud static noise to drown out the outside sounds by sheer force.
check.right: The speaker plays a precise, customized anti-sound wave specifically shaped to cancel the background murmur.

items.link: Collides with incoming noise at the eardrum.

items.answer: The peak of the outside noise meets the valley of the anti-noise and they cancel each other out.
items.why: Opposite pressures neutralize one another in the air, resulting in silence rather than louder sound.
items.scene: Two sumo wrestlers pushing against each other with identical force until both suddenly vanish into thin air.

check.wrong: The two sounds bounce off each other like billiard balls and fly away from your head.
check.right: The two opposite waves combine and flatten each other out, leaving a quiet zone at your ear.

results.topic:
Water cycle notes (Year 9 geography)
- sun heats oceans/lakes -> evaporation, water vapour rises
- plants lose water from leaves = transpiration
- vapour cools higher up -> condenses on dust -> clouds
- droplets join, get heavy -> precipitation (rain, snow, hail)
- runoff over ground into rivers, some soaks in = infiltration -> groundwater
- rivers + groundwater flow back to sea, cycle repeats

deck.title: How the Water Cycle Works
deck.subtitle: 5 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: The sun heats oceans and lakes, turning liquid water into an invisible gas called water vapour.
items.why: Solar energy breaks the bonds holding water molecules together, giving them enough energy to escape into the air.
items.scene: A giant glowing cartoon sun wearing sunglasses blows a hairdryer directly at a blue swimming pool.

check.wrong: Water evaporates because boiling bubbles push the steam up into the sky.
check.right: Water evaporates slowly at normal temperatures when individual molecules gain enough energy to escape.

items.link: Rising vapour fuels plant water loss

items.answer: Plants pull water from the soil and release it from their leaves as vapour through transpiration.
items.why: This acts like a natural pump, helping plants stay cool and moving water from the ground into the sky.
items.scene: A massive green fern sweating profusely with tiny yellow droplets pouring off every single leaf.

check.wrong: Plants sweat just like animals do to cool down their skin during hot weather.
check.right: Plants pull water up through tubes from roots to leaves, releasing it through tiny pores called stomata.

items.link: Cooling vapour condenses into clouds

items.answer: Rising water vapour cools high in the atmosphere and condenses around tiny dust specks to form clouds.
items.why: Cold air holds less moisture, forcing the gas to turn back into microscopic liquid droplets.
items.scene: A fluffy white cloud wearing a tiny winter scarf while shivering next to floating dust bunnies.

check.wrong: Clouds are giant floating sponges soaked up from oceans by the wind.
check.right: Clouds are massive collections of tiny liquid water droplets and ice crystals floating in the air.

items.link: Heavy droplets fall as rain

items.answer: Cloud droplets collide and grow heavy, eventually falling back to Earth as rain, snow, or hail.
items.why: Gravity pulls down the oversized droplets once they become too heavy for the rising air to support.
items.scene: An angry grey cloud squeezing out giant cartoon raindrops like a wet kitchen sponge.

check.wrong: Rain falls because clouds get heavy and squeeze water out like a wet cloth.
check.right: Cloud droplets grow by bumping into each other until gravity pulls them down through the air.

items.link: Water flows downhill as runoff

items.answer: Rainwater flows over the ground as runoff or soaks into the soil as infiltration to become groundwater.
items.why: Gravity guides water across the landscape, feeding rivers and filling underground spaces before returning to the sea.
items.scene: A happy puddle doing parkour down a grassy hill and diving straight into an underground sponge cave.

check.wrong: Groundwater stays trapped underground forever in deep underground lakes that never move.
check.right: Groundwater slowly flows through underground rocks and soil, eventually feeding back into rivers and oceans.

results.topic: Why is the sky blue?

deck.title: Why the sky is blue
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Sunlight looks white, but it is actually made of every color of the rainbow mixed together.
items.why: White light from the sun carries all the colors of light traveling through space as waves.
items.scene: A giant sun wearing a superhero cape made of all the colors of the rainbow, spinning around.

check.wrong: Sunlight is pure white light that contains no other colors until it hits a cloud.
check.right: Sunlight is secretly made of all the colors of the rainbow mixed together.

items.link: travels through space

items.answer: The colorful sunlight reaches Earth and crashes into tiny invisible gas pieces in the sky.
items.why: Earth is wrapped in an atmosphere full of tiny invisible bits of air called molecules that trap and bounce light.
items.scene: A million tiny bouncy green trampoline sponges floating in the air, catching bouncing laser beams.

check.wrong: Sunlight passes straight through the air without touching anything until it reaches the ground.
check.right: Sunlight crashes into tiny gas pieces floating all around in the air.

items.link: bounces off gas

items.answer: Blue light waves travel in tiny short steps, so they bounce off the gas pieces in every direction.
items.why: Short light waves bump into tiny things much easier than long red waves, making blue bounce away fast.
items.scene: Tiny blue bouncy balls pinballing everywhere in a giant room full of sleeping giant clouds.

check.wrong: Red light bounces around the most because it is the strongest color in sunlight.
check.right: Blue light bounces around the most because its waves are short and easy to scatter.

items.link: fills the sky

items.answer: All the scattered blue light spreads across the whole sky, and our eyes see it from everywhere.
items.why: When we look up, we are seeing all that bounced blue light shining down on us from the air.
items.scene: A happy child wearing giant blue sunglasses, looking up at a sky made of sparkling blue paint.

check.wrong: The sky is blue because it is acting like a giant mirror reflecting the salty ocean.
check.right: The sky is blue because air scatters blue light waves all around us.
